slides.title: TCP/IP: Concepts and IP Routing
notes: Opening slide. This course is the modernized version of the "TCP/IP Concepts" material I presented in March 1999 (Technology Week), when I was a Field Network Engineer at Cabletron Systems. The original material derived from the "Level II Routing Student Guide" (J.P. Gorsky, 1995). What changed in this edition: 16:9 format; diagrams redrawn as native, editable objects; content updated for 2026 (CIDR, IPv6, EIGRP, BGP-4, PIM-SM, MPLS, VRRPv3); RFC references revised; example addresses moved to documentation or private ranges (RFC 5737, RFC 1918, RFC 7042). Suggested duration: two days (8 hours each), with subnetting exercises and a packet-capture lab between the modules.

slides.title: Course agenda
notes: Present the two modules and the selection criterion: Module 1 covers internetworking fundamentals and routing algorithms, independent of any protocol; Module 2 applies those concepts to the TCP/IP stack (IPv4 and IPv6), to the routing protocols and to the complementary technologies (multicast, MPLS, VRRP). Topics tagged LEGACY throughout the deck are kept for their teaching value or because they still show up in certification exams, but they do not represent current practice.

slides.title: From 1999 to 2026: what changed in this course
notes: This slide is new. It calibrates expectations: almost every concept from 1999 is still valid, but the technology context changed radically. Use it to explain why some topics (Token Ring, NetWare/IPX, EGP, IGRP, MBone) now appear only as history. Data verified in October 2026: native IPv6 access to Google exceeded 50% for the first time on March 28, 2026 (50.10%, per Internet Society Pulse using Google data); in Brazil, the APNIC Labs measurement on October 5, 2026 showed about 59% of users as IPv6 capable. References: Internet Society Pulse, "18 years later, IPv6 reaches majority" (2026); APNIC Labs, IPv6 Capability Metrics, Brazil (BR).

slides.title: General routing concepts
notes: Module 1 divider. In the original, this module included objectives about the Cabletron router product line and basic Cisco router operations; both were removed as product-specific and dated. The module is now vendor neutral.

slides.title: Module 1 objectives
notes: Read the objectives with the class. By the end of the module the student should be able to explain, in their own words, why a switch and a router make decisions at different layers and why link-state algorithms converge faster than distance-vector ones. 2026 update: the original objectives 'recall the router products in the Cabletron product line' and 'basic Cisco router operations' were replaced by 'recognize Layer 2 and Layer 3 switching' and 'describe autonomous systems', topics the 1999 course already covered but did not list.

slides.title: Heterogeneity: the reason internetworks exist
notes: In the 1999 slide the heterogeneity was in the protocols: Token Ring and Ethernet segments carrying TCP/IP and NetWare at the same time. Today the heterogeneity is in the links (Ethernet, Wi-Fi, fiber, 5G, WAN) and in the administrative domains (campus, data center, public clouds), while the network layer converged on IP. The role of the interconnection devices is still the same: let stations on different links communicate as if they were on a single logical network. 2026 update: Token Ring (IEEE 802.5) and FDDI stopped being manufactured in the 2000s; NetWare/IPX was discontinued by Novell. Both appear in the original diagram and were replaced.

slides.title: Components of an internetwork
notes: Three elements build any connectionless internetwork: local links, long-distance links and the devices that interconnect them. The original listed only bridges and routers as interconnection devices; today we add Layer 2 switches (which are multiport bridges) and Layer 3 switches (routers implemented in ASIC hardware). Note that firewalls, load balancers and VPN gateways also interconnect networks, but they operate at higher layers and will be mentioned only when needed.

slides.title: Interconnection devices and the OSI model
notes: Use the diagram to fix the rule: each device decides based on the highest layer it understands. The hub repeats bits (Layer 1); the bridge/switch learns and forwards by MAC address (Layer 2); the router forwards by IP address (Layer 3). Layer 3 switches combine the last two functions in hardware. 2026 update: hubs and repeaters disappeared with switched full-duplex Ethernet; they are kept only as a Layer 1 reference.

slides.title: Bridges and Layer 2 switches
notes: The transparent bridge (IEEE 802.1D, 1990) is the direct ancestor of the Ethernet switch: a switch is a multiport bridge with hardware forwarding. The diagram shows the bridge operating only up to the data link layer: it neither reads nor changes the IP header. Key point: the bridge is 'transparent' because the stations do not know it exists; frames reach the destination with the same source and destination MAC addresses they left with.

slides.title: Frame flow through a bridge or switch
notes: Describe the learning-bridge algorithm: (1) for every frame received, the bridge records the source MAC and the arrival port in the address table (SAT, Source Address Table, today called the MAC table or CAM); (2) it looks up the destination MAC; if present in the table, it forwards out the learned port (or filters, if it is the arrival port); if absent, or if it is broadcast/multicast, it floods out all other ports; (3) every entry has an aging timer (300 s by default in IEEE 802.1D) refreshed by each frame received from that source. This is exactly the behavior of any modern Ethernet switch, just executed in ASIC with per-VLAN tables.

slides.title: Switched network: broadcast domain and Spanning Tree
notes: Example: user A wants to talk to user B through two switches. The initial communication (ARP, for instance) is a broadcast, which every switch floods. So every segment and every station receives and examines the broadcast. Once B answers, the switches have learned the MACs of A and B and forward the unicast frames only along the needed path. Redundant paths (the dashed links) are blocked by Spanning Tree to avoid Layer 2 loops, which would be catastrophic because the Ethernet frame has no TTL. 2026 update: the original STP (802.1D) took 30 to 50 s to converge; RSTP (802.1w, 2001) converges in seconds and MSTP (802.1s) handles groups of VLANs. In data centers STP was replaced by IP fabrics with EVPN/VXLAN.

slides.title: Layer 2 switching: advantages and limitations
notes: The advantages listed in 1999 are still valid: cost per port, performance and simplicity. 'Protocol independence' lost importance once IP became the only network protocol, but it is still the reason Layer 2 protocols (LLDP, STP, ARP) work across switches and not across routers. Among the limitations, broadcast storms and the failure scope remain the main argument for segmenting with routing (VLANs plus inter-VLAN routing). The old '7 bridges and 8 networks' rule was the maximum diameter 802.1D recommended so that the STP timers would work; with RSTP and star topologies that rule is no longer applied as a hard limit, but the principle (keep the broadcast domain small) stands. 2026 update: 'bridges drop oversized packets' referred to the different MTUs of Token Ring (up to 17,914 bytes) and Ethernet (1,500); with universal Ethernet and jumbo frames the problem practically disappeared.

slides.title: Routers
notes: The router performs its function at the network layer. Unlike the bridge, it makes the forwarding decision from the destination network (IP) address, rewrites the data-link headers at every hop and takes part in a distributed algorithm to compute the paths. Explain the phrase 'allows multiple paths': unlike STP, which blocks redundant links, IP routing uses all the links and can even load-balance across equal-cost paths (ECMP).

slides.title: End systems and intermediate systems
notes: ISO terminology: end systems (the hosts) implement all the layers; intermediate systems (the routers) implement only up to the network layer. The transport connection (TCP) is end to end and crosses the routers without being interpreted by them. This explains why reliability (retransmission, flow control) is the hosts' responsibility, and why a router may drop packets under congestion: TCP at the endpoints will notice and react.

slides.title: Data flow inside a router
notes: The original diagram showed a 1999 router: a hardware buffer per interface, a software buffer, the routing table, the ARP cache and a hold queue. The 2026 version separates control plane and data plane: the control plane (CPU) runs the routing protocols and builds the RIB (routing table); from it derives the FIB, the compact table the data plane (ASIC or optimized software) uses to forward at line rate. The adjacency table (ARP/ND) supplies ready-made data-link headers. Step by step: the frame arrives, the data-link header is removed, the IP packet is validated (checksum, TTL), the FIB is consulted by longest prefix, the TTL is decremented, a new data-link header is built and the frame is queued on the egress interface (where QoS policies act).

slides.title: Routers: advantages and limitations
notes: Compare with the switch slide. The router's main advantage is bounding the broadcast and failure domain; its main historical disadvantage was performance, because in 1999 routing was done in software on a general-purpose CPU. Today Layer 3 switches and core routers forward in ASIC at line rate, so the throughput argument has practically vanished; what remains is configuration complexity and cost. 'Protocol dependence' also stopped being a practical problem: a modern router only needs to handle IPv4 and IPv6 (dual stack).

slides.title: Routable and nonroutable protocols
notes: A protocol is 'routable' when it has a network layer with hierarchical logical addressing (network + node), letting routers forward its packets between different links. In 1999 this mattered because corporate networks carried several protocols at once; the routers of the day (Cabletron, Cisco) routed IP, IPX, AppleTalk and DECnet simultaneously. In 2026 the list shrank to IPv4 and IPv6. The nonroutable protocols (NetBIOS/NetBEUI, SNA, LAT, MOP) either disappeared or were encapsulated over IP (NetBIOS over TCP/IP, RFC 1001/1002; SNA over DLSw or Enterprise Extender). The concept, however, is still useful: Layer 2 protocols such as ARP, STP and LLDP stay confined to the link and do not cross routers.

slides.title: Addressing: network layer versus data link layer
notes: Two address spaces coexist in every internetwork: the data-link address (MAC, 48 bits on Ethernet and Wi-Fi), which identifies the interface within a link and comes burned in by the manufacturer (or is locally assigned), and the network address (IP), logical and hierarchical, which identifies the system across the whole internetwork and is assigned by the administrator or by DHCP/SLAAC. The network address has two components: the network part (prefix), which the router uses to decide the next hop, and the node (host) part, which identifies the interface within that network. The mapping between the two spaces is done by ARP (IPv4) or Neighbor Discovery (IPv6).

slides.title: Packet transmission: down the stack
notes: Follow the diagram top to bottom on the sender and bottom to top on the receiver: the transport layer hands a segment to the network layer, which adds the IP header and forms the packet (datagram); the data-link layer encapsulates the packet in a frame with a header (MACs and EtherType) and a trailer (FCS); the physical layer transmits the bits. In the original Ethernet and in IEEE 802.3 with LLC/SNAP there was an LLC sublayer between the network and MAC layers (the 1999 slide showed LLC-PDU and MAC-PDU). Today practically all IP over Ethernet uses the Ethernet II (DIX) format with an EtherType field (0x0800 for IPv4, 0x86DD for IPv6), without LLC; the LLC sublayer survives in Wi-Fi (802.11 uses LLC/SNAP).

slides.title: Encapsulation: an IPv4 packet inside an Ethernet frame
notes: The Ethernet II frame carries: preamble (7 bytes) and start frame delimiter (SFD, 1 byte), destination MAC, source MAC, EtherType (2 bytes) and a data field of 46 to 1,500 bytes, followed by the FCS (CRC-32). Inside the data field goes the IP packet: a 20-byte header (without options) and a payload of up to 65,535 bytes in total, which forces fragmentation whenever the packet exceeds the 1,500-byte MTU. The IPv4 header is detailed in Module 2. Note already that the Type of Service (ToS) field of the original slide was redefined as DSCP + ECN (RFC 2474 and RFC 3168).

slides.title: Routing algorithms: how routers learn about networks
notes: Opening question: how does a router discover every network and subnet in an internetwork? Two methods: manual configuration (static routes) or automatic distribution by a distributed adaptive (dynamic) routing protocol. In practice both are used: static routes for leaf networks and the default route; dynamic protocols for the core. The next slides walk through: static routing, dynamic routing, distance vector (with its problems and fixes) and link state.

slides.title: Static routing
notes: All routing information is precomputed by the administrator and entered manually. If the topology changes, someone must recompute and reconfigure. That is why static routing does not scale to large, dynamic internetworks, yet it is still the right choice for stub (leaf) networks, which have a single way out. Diagram example: network A sits behind R2, with a single link to R1. On R2 a default route pointing to R1 is enough; on R1 a static route to network A via R2 is enough. No dynamic protocol needs to run on that link. 2026 update: static routes can be conditioned on reachability checks (IP SLA, BFD) and are widely used at Internet edges and in public clouds (VPC route tables).

slides.title: Distributed adaptive (dynamic) routing
notes: Routers dynamically sense their local environment (active interfaces, neighbors) and exchange that information among themselves in a distributed fashion, with no central controller. Together they run a distributed algorithm that determines the optimal route between any two stations. Two families dominate the interior protocols: distance vector (each router tells its neighbors 'how far I am from each destination') and link state (each router tells everyone 'these are my links and their costs', and each one computes the complete map). BGP, used between autonomous systems, is a path vector: it advertises the list of ASs traversed.

slides.title: Distance-vector routing
notes: Each router keeps, for every known destination, the distance (metric) and the neighbor through which it is reached (the vector). Periodically it sends its whole table to its direct neighbors (RIP: every 30 s). On receiving an update from a neighbor, the router updates its table when: (1) the destination was unknown; (2) the new route is shorter than the known one; (3) the current route already goes through that neighbor and the advertised distance changed (up or down), in which case the change is accepted even if it is worse. The third case is what lets the news that a destination got worse or went down propagate, and it is also the entry point of the count-to-infinity problem, shown next.

slides.title: Routing metrics
notes: A metric is the way to measure the 'distance' between source and destination. Hop count (RIP) is the simplest, but it ignores link capacity: in the diagram, the two-hop path over 1 Gbps links is better than one hop over a 2 Mbps link. That is why EIGRP uses bandwidth and delay, and OSPF/IS-IS use an administrative cost derived from bandwidth. 2026 update: the original speeds (56 kbps, 1.544 Mbps T1, 10 Mbps) were replaced by current values, but the lesson is the same.

slides.title: The slow convergence problem (count to infinity)
notes: Initial scenario: three routers in a row; R1 is directly connected to network A (metric 0 or 1, depending on the protocol), R2 reaches A via R1 (metric 1) and R3 via R2 (metric 2). Everyone periodically advertises their tables to their neighbors: R1 says 'A: 0', R2 says 'A: 1', R3 says 'A: 2'. With advertisements in every direction (no split horizon), R2 also receives from R3 that 'A is at 2 via R3', which it ignores for now because its current route (1 via R1) is better.

slides.title: Slow convergence: the failure creates a loop
notes: The link from R1 to network A goes down. R1 marks A as unreachable (infinite metric, 16 in RIP). Before R1 advertises that, R2 receives (or already had) from R3 the advertisement 'A: 2'. Having lost its route via R1 (or receiving 'A: 16' from R1), R2 accepts R3's route: 'A: 3 via R3'. But R3 reached A via R2! A loop has formed: packets for A go R2 → R3 → R2 → R3 until the TTL expires. Worse: in the following updates, R2 advertises 'A: 3' to R3, which moves to 'A: 4 via R2', which advertises 'A: 4' to R2, which goes to 5, and so on until the metric reaches infinity (16 in RIP, which is why the limit is so low). This is count to infinity; with updates every 30 s, it can take minutes.

slides.title: Fix 1: split horizon
notes: Rule: never advertise a route back out the interface you learned it from. In the three-routers-in-a-row example, router B learned 10.0 and 20.0 from A, so it does not advertise them back to A; it learned 40.0 from C, so it does not advertise it to C. R3 would therefore never tell R2 'A: 2', and the loop of the previous slide never forms. The diagram shows what each router advertises in each direction with simple split horizon. Note that split horizon solves loops between two direct neighbors, but not loops with three or more routers in a ring; that is why it is combined with hold-down and triggered updates. Addresses updated to the private range 172.16.0.0/12 (RFC 1918); the original used 134.141.x.0, a block that belonged to Cabletron at the time.

slides.title: Fix 2: split horizon with poison reverse
notes: A more aggressive variant: instead of omitting the route learned on an interface, the router advertises it back out that interface with an infinite metric (16 in RIP). B tells A: '10.0 and 20.0 are unreachable through me', making it explicit that A must not use B to reach them, even if A loses its route. The cost is larger updates (every route is advertised on every interface). The benefit is breaking loops faster, including some that simple split horizon does not prevent.

slides.title: Fix 3: hold-down timer
notes: On receiving the information that a network became unreachable, the router enters hold-down for that destination: for a fixed time (180 s in Cisco's RIP) it ignores advertisements claiming the network is back with an equal or worse metric, accepting only better advertisements or ones from the original neighbor. The idea is to wait long enough for the news of the failure to reach everyone, avoiding the acceptance of stale information still circulating. Side effect: the convergence of a route that really came back is delayed by the same amount. That is why modern protocols prefer mechanisms that do not depend on long timers (EIGRP with DUAL, link state with SPF).

slides.title: Fix 4: triggered updates
notes: Instead of waiting for the next periodic advertisement (30 s in RIP), the router sends an update immediately whenever its table changes, containing only the routes that changed. This speeds up the propagation of bad news and shrinks the window during which stale information can cause loops. Combined, the four techniques (split horizon, poison reverse, hold-down and triggered updates) make RIP usable in small networks. In EIGRP every update is triggered and there are no periodic table advertisements: the adjacency is kept by Hello packets and information is exchanged reliably (RTP).

slides.title: Distance vector, example (1 of 4): initial state
notes: Four routers in a row (A, B, C, D) interconnect five networks (1 to 5). Before any exchange of information, each router knows only the directly connected networks (DC, metric 1 by the convention of this example). The next four slides show the tables after each update cycle, with simple split horizon active. Ask the students to predict the contents of the tables before advancing each slide.

slides.title: Distance vector, example (2 of 4): first exchange
notes: First exchange of advertisements, with simple split horizon. A receives network 3 from B (metric 2 via B); network 2, which both have as directly connected, stays at metric 1 in each. B receives network 1 from A and network 4 from C; C receives network 2 from B and network 5 from D; D receives network 3 from C. Each router now knows the networks one neighbor away. The new entries of each cycle are highlighted (in the 1999 original they were marked in blue).

slides.title: Distance vector, example (3 of 4): second exchange
notes: In the second periodic update, B advertises networks 3 and 4 to A (A already had 3; it adds 4 at metric 3 via B); C advertises network 5 to B (metric 3 via C); B advertises network 1 to C (metric 3 via B); C advertises network 2 to D (metric 3 via C). Note that A and D, at the ends, still do not know the whole topology: A is missing network 5 and D is missing network 1.

slides.title: Distance vector, example (4 of 4): convergence
notes: In the third exchange, A learns network 5 (metric 4 via B) and D learns network 1 (metric 4 via C). Now every table contains all five networks: the network converged in three iterations. In general, a network with a diameter of N hops needs N-1 update cycles to converge, which, with RIP's 30 s period, can mean minutes. That slowness is the motivation for triggered updates and for link-state protocols.

slides.title: Link-state routing: principles (1 of 2)
notes: Four responsibilities of each router: (1) discover its neighbors and learn their names (identifiers), usually by Hello packets; (2) build a link-state packet (LSA, Link State Advertisement, or LSP in IS-IS) with the list of neighbors and the cost of each link; (3) flood the LSA to every router in the area, each one keeping the most recent LSA from each originator, forming an identical database everywhere; (4) with the complete map, compute the routes to each destination with the SPF algorithm (Dijkstra), with itself as the root.

slides.title: Link-state routing: principles (2 of 2)
notes: The essential difference from distance vector: a link-state router never sends 'lists of destinations with distances'. It does only two things: actively tests the state of its neighbors (Hello) and propagates periodically (and immediately on every change) the description of its own links. On receiving an LSA, it updates the map by marking links up or down; on every change it recomputes the routes with Dijkstra. In OSPF the LSA is also re-sent every 30 minutes (LSRefreshTime) and expires after 60 minutes (MaxAge), which keeps the database consistent even without changes.

slides.title: Link state: advantages over distance vector
notes: Three advantages: (1) each router computes the routes independently from the same raw topology data, instead of trusting the neighbor's arithmetic; (2) it converges faster, because a router can recognize a new LSA and forward it even before recomputing its routes, so the news spreads at flooding speed; (3) it scales better, because each LSA carries only the direct connections of one router (small, stable information), and areas limit the scope of flooding. Costs: more memory (LSDB) and CPU (SPF), and more careful configuration (areas). On 2026 hardware those costs are irrelevant for networks of thousands of routers.

slides.title: Link-state protocols in use
notes: In 1999 there were three interior link-state protocols: OSPF (IETF, for IP; then RFC 1247, today RFC 2328 for OSPFv2 and RFC 5340 for OSPFv3), IS-IS (ISO 10589, designed at Digital for DECnet Phase V and extended to IP by RFC 1195) and NLSP (Novell, for IPX). NLSP died with IPX. OSPF and IS-IS remain the market's two link-state IGPs: OSPF dominates in enterprise networks; IS-IS is widely used by service providers and in large data centers, thanks to its independence from IP and its extensibility (TLVs), which also made it the base of Segment Routing.

slides.title: Autonomous system (AS)
notes: Classic definition (RFC 1930): a set of routers and networks under a common administration, with a single, coherent routing policy toward the outside. Inside the AS runs an IGP (OSPF, IS-IS, EIGRP, RIP); between ASs runs the Internet's de facto EGP, BGP-4. Each public AS receives a number (ASN) assigned by the regional registries (in Brazil, NIC.br/Registro.br together with LACNIC; in the US, ARIN). 2026 update: ASNs were 16 bits (up to 65,535); since RFC 4893 (2007), consolidated in RFC 6793 (2012), they are 32 bits. Private ranges: 64512 to 65534 and 4,200,000,000 to 4,294,967,294 (RFC 6996). Examples: AS 2 (UDEL), AS 15169 (Google), AS 28573 (Claro Brazil).

(TTL); (2) what information does a distance-vector router send to its neighbors, and a link-state one? (3) name the four techniques that mitigate count to infinity; (4) what is an autonomous system and which protocol runs between them?

notes: Original objectives kept, with updated terminology: 'IPng' became IPv6; 'IGRP' became EIGRP; and we added IS-IS, BGP-4 and the modern IPv6 mechanisms (Neighbor Discovery, SLAAC).

slides.title: Module 2 objectives (2 of 2)

slides.title: TCP/IP: origin and governance
notes: TCP/IP came out of a project funded by ARPA/DARPA of the US Department of Defense; the seminal paper by Cerf and Kahn is from 1974, the IP (RFC 791) and TCP (RFC 793) specifications are from September 1981, and the ARPANET switched to TCP/IP on January 1, 1983. The specifications are published as RFCs (Requests for Comments), public documents maintained by the RFC Editor; standardization is done by the IETF (since 1986) and the numbers (ports, protocols, addresses) are administered by IANA. 2026 update: the TCP specification was consolidated in 2022 in RFC 9293, which replaces RFC 793 and dozens of updates. The TCP/IP suite does not define only Layers 3 and 4: it includes applications (DNS, HTTP, SMTP, SSH...) and auxiliary protocols (ICMP, ARP, DHCP).

slides.title: The TCP/IP protocol stack and the OSI model
notes: The TCP/IP stack has four layers (RFC 1122): application, transport, Internet and network interface (link). Many courses show five, separating physical from data link. The seven-layer OSI model is useful as vocabulary: OSI Layers 5 to 7 correspond to the TCP/IP application layer; OSI Layer 3 is the Internet layer; Layers 2 and 1 form the network interface. The media access protocols listed in the original (Ethernet, Token Ring, FDDI) were updated: today, Ethernet, Wi-Fi and WAN links of every kind.

slides.title: Application layer
notes: The original slide listed WWW, file transfer (TFTP, FTP, NFS), e-mail (SMTP), remote login (Telnet, rlogin) and management (SNMP). In 2026: the Web uses HTTPS (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 over QUIC) almost exclusively; cleartext Telnet, rlogin and FTP were replaced by SSH, SFTP and HTTPS; DNS gained DNSSEC and encrypted transports (DoT, DoH); e-mail uses submission on port 587 with STARTTLS/TLS and IMAPS. Highlight: TLS is not a formal OSI layer, but it sits between application and transport; most application protocols run over TLS today.

slides.title: Transport layer
notes: TCP (RFC 9293) offers a reliable, ordered byte stream with flow and congestion control, connection oriented (three-way handshake). UDP (RFC 768) offers connectionless datagrams with no guarantees and a minimal 8-byte overhead: ideal for DNS, voice, video, games and for protocols that implement their own control. The relevant newcomer since 1999 is QUIC (RFC 9000, 2021), a transport over UDP with integrated TLS 1.3 encryption, stream multiplexing without head-of-line blocking and connection establishment in 0 or 1 RTT; it is the base of HTTP/3. SCTP (RFC 9260) is used in telephony signaling and mobile networks.

slides.title: Internet layer
notes: The original listed IP, ARP, RARP and ICMP. Update: IPv4 (RFC 791) and IPv6 (RFC 8200) coexist in dual stack; ICMP (RFC 792) and ICMPv6 (RFC 4443) handle diagnostics and error signaling, and ICMPv6 also carries Neighbor Discovery (ND, RFC 4861), which replaces ARP in IPv6; IGMP (RFC 3376) and MLD (RFC 3810) manage multicast groups; IPsec (AH, ESP) protects packets. RARP (RFC 903) was replaced by BOOTP and then DHCP. ARP, although listed in the Internet layer for convenience, operates between Layers 2 and 3: it is encapsulated directly in Ethernet frames (EtherType 0x0806), not in IP.

slides.title: The IPv4 datagram in detail
notes: Walk through the fields: Version (4); IHL, header length in 32-bit words (5 = 20 bytes, up to 15 = 60 bytes with options); DSCP and ECN, the former 'Type of Service' (RFC 2474 and RFC 3168), used for QoS and congestion notification; Total Length in bytes (maximum 65,535); Identification, Flags (DF: don't fragment; MF: more fragments) and Offset, used in fragmentation; TTL, decremented by every router and which, on reaching zero, causes a drop and an ICMP Time Exceeded (the basis of traceroute); Protocol, which identifies the payload (next slide); Checksum, of the header only; source and destination addresses; options (rare and frequently blocked). Practical note: fragmentation is avoided with Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191) by setting DF; in IPv6 routers never fragment.

slides.title: Protocol numbers: identifying the IP payload
notes: The Protocol field (IPv4) or Next Header (IPv6) tells the Internet layer whom to hand the data to: 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP, 1 for ICMP and so on. It is the first stage of demultiplexing; the second is the port, inside the TCP/UDP segment. The values are administered by IANA in the 'Protocol Numbers' registry (RFC 1700 from 1994, cited in the original, was replaced by the online registries, RFC 3232). Draw attention to 41 (IPv6 encapsulated in IPv4, used in 6in4 tunnels), 47 (GRE), 50 and 51 (IPsec), 58 (ICMPv6), 88 (EIGRP), 89 (OSPF), 103 (PIM), 112 (VRRP) and 132 (SCTP), all seen throughout the course.

slides.title: Port numbers: identifying the application
notes: TCP and UDP (and also SCTP and QUIC) use 16-bit ports to tell applications apart on the same host. RFC 6335 defines three ranges: system ports (0 to 1023, the 'well-known' ones), registered user ports (1024 to 49151) and dynamic or ephemeral ports (49152 to 65535), used on the client side. The official registry is IANA's 'Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry', which replaced RFC 1060 cited in the original (later RFC 1700). A socket is identified by the 5-tuple: protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port; that is what NAT, firewalls and load balancers track.

slides.title: Receiving a frame: demultiplexing at three levels
notes: Follow the frame from the bottom up: (1) the interface checks the FCS and the destination MAC (its own, broadcast or a subscribed multicast) and uses the EtherType to hand the payload to the right protocol (0x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP, 0x8100 802.1Q, 0x8847 MPLS); (2) the IP layer validates the header and uses the Protocol field to deliver to TCP, UDP, ICMP, etc.; (3) the transport uses the destination port to deliver to the right application (DNS on 53, SSH on 22). In 1999 the Type/SNAP ID field played the EtherType role; the original diagram showed Telnet 23, FTP 21, DNS 53 and TFTP 69.

slides.title: Decimal-to-binary conversion
notes: Basic tool for subnetting: each octet has 8 bits with weights 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. To convert 172 to binary, subtract the largest weights that fit: 172 - 128 = 44; 44 - 32 = 12; 12 - 8 = 4; 4 - 4 = 0, so bits 128, 32, 8 and 4 are on: 10101100. The sum of all weights is 255, the largest value of an octet. Ask the students to convert 192, 224, 240, 248, 252, 254 and 255 (the values that appear in masks) and to memorize that each one adds a 1 bit on the left.

slides.title: The IPv4 address
notes: Every IPv4 interface has a 32-bit address, written as four decimal numbers separated by dots (dotted-decimal notation), each representing one octet. When IP was standardized in 1981 the address had two parts, network and host; the network part was assigned by the numbering authorities (today IANA → RIRs → providers → organizations) and the host part by the network administrator. The original example, 134.141.20.10, was a real Cabletron address; we use 172.16.20.10, from the RFC 1918 private range.

slides.title: Classful addressing (1981 to 1993)
notes: Originally there were three classes of networks, A, B and C, recognized by the first bits of the first octet (the first-octet rule): class A, leading bit 0, 7 network bits and 24 host bits (1 to 126; 0 and 127 reserved); class B, bits 10, 14 network bits and 16 host bits (128 to 191); class C, bits 110, 21 network bits and 8 host bits (192 to 223). Class D (1110, 224 to 239) was defined later for multicast (RFC 1112) and class E (1111, 240 to 255) stayed reserved. The scheme was abandoned in 1993 in favor of CIDR (RFC 1519, today RFC 4632) because it wasted addresses (a class B for a company with 300 hosts) and made the Internet routing table explode with class C networks. The terms 'class A/B/C' survive only as jargon and in certification exams; modern equipment is classless by default.

slides.title: CIDR: classless routing and prefix notation
notes: With CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing), the boundary between network and host is given explicitly by the prefix length (/n = n network bits), equivalent to a mask of n contiguous 1 bits. This allows allocating blocks of the right size (172.16.20.0/23 for 510 hosts, instead of a class B) and aggregating (summarizing) several prefixes into a single routing advertisement, shrinking the Internet tables (supernetting). In 2026 the global IPv4 table has about one million prefixes; without CIDR it would be unmanageable. VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Mask) is the same principle applied inside an organization: subnets of different sizes according to need. Classful protocols (RIPv1, IGRP) do not carry a mask and do not support VLSM; every modern protocol (RIPv2, EIGRP, OSPF, IS-IS, BGP-4) is classless.

slides.title: Special-purpose IPv4 addresses
notes: The original listed four cases: 0.0.0.0 ('this host on this network', source only, e.g., a DHCP client), 255.255.255.255 (limited broadcast, destination only, does not cross routers), directed broadcast (all host bits set to 1, e.g., 172.16.20.255/24) and 127.x.y.z (loopback, never leaves the host). The list grew: private addresses (RFC 1918) used with NAT; shared address space 100.64.0.0/10 for provider CGNAT (RFC 6598); link-local 169.254.0.0/16 (APIPA, RFC 3927); documentation blocks (RFC 5737), which we use in this course; multicast 224.0.0.0/4; and the former class E 240.0.0.0/4, still not usable on the Internet. The consolidated registry is RFC 6890 and IANA's 'Special-Purpose Address Registry'.

slides.title: Subnets: a third level of hierarchy
notes: In 1984/1985 (RFC 917 and RFC 950, Internet Standard Subnetting Procedure) a third level was added to the address structure: the subnet. The organization receives a prefix (back then, a class network) and borrows bits from the host part to number its internal subnets, one per link. To the rest of the Internet the network is still a single one; internally the routers distinguish the subnets. The subnet field can have any size (RFC 950 asked for at least 2 bits; today, with CIDR, any value), and it is defined by a 32-bit mask.

slides.title: The subnet mask and the comparison under mask
notes: The mask is a 32-bit pattern with 1s in the network and subnet positions and 0s in the host positions. The fundamental operation is the comparison under mask: a bitwise AND between the address and the mask; every address bit whose mask bit is 0 is zeroed, and the result is the subnet identifier, which is compared with that of the route or of the host itself. The current specification requires contiguous masks (all 1s on the left); noncontiguous masks were allowed in RFC 950 but were never practical and have been forbidden since RFC 1519. This operation is executed by every host when sending a packet (local or remote?) and by every router when consulting its table (longest prefix match).

slides.title: Comparison under mask: example
notes: Host 172.16.128.2 with mask 255.255.255.0 (/24). Write address and mask in binary, AND column by column and convert back: 172.16.128.0. That is the subnet identifier. The 'network' in the old sense (class B) would be 172.16.0.0; the subnet, 172.16.128.0. With CIDR we simply say the host belongs to prefix 172.16.128.0/24. The original used 134.141.128.2; the logic is identical.

slides.title: Addressing with subnets in an internetwork
notes: The diagram shows an autonomous system that received the prefix 172.16.0.0/16 and divided it into /24 subnets, one per link: 172.16.10.0/24, .20.0, .30.0, .40.0 and .50.0. To the Internet only the aggregate 172.16.0.0/16 is advertised (in this example, being private, it would not even be advertised; imagine a public block). Internally, the routers exchange the subnets through the IGP. Every router interface gets an address in the subnet of the link it is attached to; by convention the first or the last usable address.

slides.title: Host addressing with subnets
notes: Two links joined by a router: 172.16.128.0/24 on interface E0 (172.16.128.1) and 172.16.64.0/24 on E1 (172.16.64.1). The hosts on each side get addresses in their subnet and use the router's address as default gateway. The breakdown of address 172.16.128.2 shows the three levels: network 172.16, subnet 128, host 2. Question for the class: can host 172.16.128.2 talk directly to 172.16.64.2? No: the comparison under mask yields different subnets, so the packet goes to the gateway (next slides).

slides.title: Special addresses in a subnetted environment
notes: Within each subnet, the address with all host bits set to 1 is the directed broadcast of that subnet (172.16.128.255 for 172.16.128.0/24) and the address with all host bits set to 0 identifies the subnet itself; neither can be assigned to a host. That is why the number of usable hosts is 2^(host bits) - 2. Two important updates: (1) RFC 950 recommended not using the first ('subnet zero') and the last ('all-ones') subnets of a block; that fell with CIDR (RFC 1878) and all modern equipment uses them; (2) RFC 3021 (2000) allows /31 on point-to-point links, with two addresses and no broadcast, doubling the efficiency versus /30; and /32 is used for loopbacks.

slides.title: Masks off the octet boundary (VLSM)
notes: When the number of subnet bits does not fall on an octet boundary, you must work in binary. Example: 203.0.113.77 with mask 255.255.255.248 (/29): the last octet 77 = 01001101; the mask 248 = 11111000 keeps the first five bits (01001 = 72) and zeroes the three host bits. So the subnet is 203.0.113.72/29, the hosts go from .73 to .78 and the broadcast is .79. The 'step' between /29 subnets is 256 - 248 = 8: .0, .8, .16, ..., .72, .80. The original used 197.129.59.77 with five subnet bits on a class C; the arithmetic is the same. With VLSM, a /24 block can be split into subnets of different sizes, as the next slide shows.

slides.title: VLSM in practice: addressing plan for a /24
notes: Model exercise: split 172.16.20.0/24 to serve a network of 100 users, one of 50 servers, one of 25 management devices, one of 10 printers and four point-to-point links. Golden rule of VLSM: allocate from the largest to the smallest subnet, always on boundaries aligned to the block size. 172.16.20.252/30 is left over and, if the links use /31, even more space. Ask the students to redo the plan with /31 on the links (RFC 3021) and to discuss where to place the gateway address in each subnet.

slides.title: Internet Protocol behavior
notes: This part follows the original slide by slide: host communication, route determination, local and remote destinations, gateway lookup, and then ARP in three scenarios (local host, remote host, Proxy ARP). We close with a complete data-transfer example across two routers.

slides.title: IP host communication: always two steps
notes: Every IP communication starts with two steps on the source host: (1) route determination: is the destination local (same link) or remote (behind a router)? If remote, what is the next hop? (2) address resolution: what is the MAC of the destination (if local) or of the next hop (if remote)? These steps always happen, on every operating system and in every topology, even when the administrator never thought about them; they are the basis for troubleshooting 'I can't ping'.

slides.title: Route determination: local or remote?
notes: The first step is deciding whether the destination IP is local or remote. Local destination: it is within the same prefix (network or subnet) as the source host; remote destination: it is outside that prefix. The host uses three pieces of information: its own IP address, its mask (prefix) and the destination IP address. It applies the mask to both addresses (comparison under mask) and compares the results. Note for 2026: modern hosts do this by consulting their route table with longest prefix match, which is equivalent to the comparison under mask when there is only the connected-subnet route and the default route.

slides.title: Route determination logic
notes: The flowchart from the original: IF (destination IP AND source mask) = (source IP AND source mask) THEN the destination is on the same physical link and the source can send directly; ELSE the source consults its route table to find the next hop (gateway) and sends the packets to it. In both cases, the next step is address resolution (ARP) for the chosen IP: the destination or the gateway.

slides.title: Local or remote: example with AND
notes: Source 172.16.128.7, mask 255.255.255.0, destination 172.16.128.2. AND of the destination with the mask: 172.16.128.0; AND of the source with the mask: 172.16.128.0. Equal results, so the destination is local. Repeat with destination 172.16.64.2: the AND gives 172.16.64.0, different from 172.16.128.0, so remote. The original used 134.141.128.x.

slides.title: Local destinations
notes: If the destination network and the source network are the same, communication happens without a router: the frames are transmitted directly on the link both stations are attached to. The host moves immediately to the address resolution phase to obtain the destination's MAC. Note that 'same link' today means, in practice, 'same VLAN': Layer 2 switches between the stations are transparent.

slides.title: Remote destinations
notes: If the source determines that the destination is remote, there is an intermediate step before address resolution: the next-hop gateway lookup. It determines which router the source will use to forward packets to the remote network. Only then does the source ARP, and it ARPs for the gateway, not for the destination.

slides.title: Next-hop gateway lookup
notes: The source station consults its route table to determine the next hop for the remote network. A host's table may be built from static routes, from the default gateway (received by DHCP or RA) or, on servers and routers, from dynamic protocols. The result is the IP address of a directly connected router (on the same link) able to forward toward the destination. The lookup follows the longest-prefix rule: among all routes matching the destination, the most specific wins; the default route (/0) matches everything and wins last.

slides.title: IP communication: what the host knows at this point
notes: Intermediate summary. The source host has determined (1) whether the destination is local or remote and (2), if remote, the logical address of the next hop. It has all the network-layer information. What is missing is the data-link-layer information: the MAC of the destination or of the gateway. That is where ARP comes in.

slides.title: Address resolution: ARP (RFC 826)
notes: Whether the destination is direct or the gateway, transmission on the link is always MAC to MAC. The source must resolve the MAC corresponding to the chosen IP before transmitting. IP uses ARP (Address Resolution Protocol, RFC 826, 1982) to obtain the IP → MAC mapping: it sends a question in broadcast ('who has IP X?') and the owner answers in unicast with its MAC. Every host keeps an ARP cache with the learned mappings, so it does not have to ask for every packet. ARP is encapsulated directly in Ethernet (EtherType 0x0806), not in IP, and only works within the link: routers do not forward ARP. In IPv6 the role belongs to Neighbor Discovery (ND, RFC 4861), using ICMPv6 and multicast.

slides.title: ARP, local host example (1 of 6): the scenario
notes: Host A (172.16.10.1/24) has never communicated with host B (172.16.10.200/24) and wants to open an SSH session to it. (The original used Telnet; SSH is the modern equivalent.) A's TCP/IP stack runs the route determination logic to find out whether B is local or remote. Point out that, from ARP's point of view, the application hardly matters: the process is the same for any IP packet.

slides.title: ARP, local host example (2 of 6): B is local; empty cache
notes: The AND of the destination IP and of the source IP with A's mask gives the same result, 172.16.10.0: B is local. A looks in its ARP cache for the mapping of 172.16.10.200, but the cache is empty (or the entry expired). A needs to ask the network.

slides.title: ARP, local host (3 of 6): ARP Request in broadcast
notes: A transmits an ARP Request encapsulated in an Ethernet frame with a broadcast destination (FF-FF-FF-FF-FF-FF) and EtherType 0x0806. Every station on the link (on the VLAN) receives the frame and hands its contents to the ARP software, which compares the 'target IP' with its own. On a VLAN with hundreds of hosts, every ARP Request interrupts all of them: that is why large broadcast domains cost CPU on every station.

slides.title: The ARP Request packet
notes: ARP format (28 bytes for Ethernet/IPv4): hardware type (1 = Ethernet), protocol type (0x0800 = IPv4), hardware address length (6) and protocol address length (4), operation (1 = request, 2 = reply), sender MAC and IP, target MAC and IP. In the request, the target MAC is unknown (filled with zeros). The Ethernet frame carrying it has a broadcast destination, source = A's MAC and EtherType 0x0806; the data field is padded up to 46 bytes.

slides.title: ARP, local host example (4 of 6): B processes the request
notes: B's MAC layer hands the ARP Request to the ARP software in B's IP stack. ARP recognizes the target IP (172.16.10.200) as its own. The other stations (C) silently discard the request, because the target IP is not theirs. B then builds an ARP Reply and hands it to the MAC layer for transmission. Many implementations take the opportunity to record A's IP/MAC pair in B's cache, since they will probably answer A right away.

slides.title: ARP, local host example (5 of 6): ARP Reply in unicast
notes: B's ARP software sends the reply to A, providing B's MAC. The reply is unicast: an Ethernet frame from MAC B to MAC A (B learned A's MAC from the request itself). Depending on the stack, B also stores A's mapping in its ARP cache, avoiding an ARP Request in the reverse direction when answering the SSH session.

slides.title: The ARP Reply packet
notes: In the reply, the operation is 2 and the sender and target fields are filled with B's data (sender) and A's data (target). The Ethernet frame is unicast: destination = A's MAC, source = B's MAC, EtherType 0x0806. On receiving it, A installs the entry 172.16.10.200 → 00-00-5E-00-53-0B in its cache.

slides.title: ARP, local host example (6 of 6): communication proceeds
notes: On receiving the ARP Reply, A's ARP process installs B's entry in the cache. A's stack now has everything it needs: the destination IP (network layer) and the destination MAC (data link layer). The SSH segment that was queued is encapsulated and transmitted; the next packets use the cache, with no new ARP, until the entry expires.

slides.title: ARP, remote host example (1 of 4): the scenario
notes: Same intent (A wants SSH to B), but now B is on another subnet: A is 172.16.10.1/24 and B is 172.16.100.1/24. A is configured with the subnet mask (/24) and with a default gateway, router R1 (172.16.10.254). The default gateway provides A with a next hop for every destination outside its local segment.

slides.title: ARP, remote host example (2 of 4): B is remote
notes: By the route determination logic, A concludes that B is remote: 172.16.100.1 AND /24 = 172.16.100.0, different from 172.16.10.0. A must then perform the next-hop lookup to find a router able to reach the remote subnet.

slides.title: ARP, remote host (3 of 4): default route and ARP for the gateway
notes: The default gateway configuration created a default route entry in A's route table (0.0.0.0/0 via 172.16.10.254). A's stack believes R1 is the next hop for ALL remote destinations. Essential consequence: A ARPs for R1's local interface (172.16.10.254), not for B. An ARP for B would never be answered, since the broadcast does not cross R1.

slides.title: ARP, remote host example (4 of 4): communication via R1
notes: Once the MAC of R1's local interface is resolved, A's communication with B goes, at the data link layer, through the router's interface: frames from MAC A to MAC R1, carrying IP packets from 172.16.10.1 to 172.16.100.1. R1 receives the frames, discards the Ethernet header and routes by the destination network address. On B's link, R1 does its own ARP for B. A's cache will hold R1; R1's will hold A and B.

slides.title: Proxy ARP
notes: Proxy ARP (RFC 1027) is an extension of ARP that routers can run: answering ARP requests on behalf of hosts on other subnets. It was created to minimize the routing knowledge hosts needed in a subnetted network: hosts configured with the 'natural' mask (no subnets, no gateway) think everyone is on the same link and ARP for any destination; the router answers with its own MAC and forwards the traffic. Today it is rarely necessary (DHCP delivers mask and gateway), but it still exists in a few scenarios and is a classic source of strange behavior when left enabled without need.

slides.title: Proxy ARP, example (1 of 3): host with a 'flat' mask
notes: Host A has address 172.16.10.1 with the natural mask 255.255.0.0 (/16) and no gateway. It wants to open SSH to B (172.16.100.1), which is actually on another /24 subnet behind R1. By the route determination logic, with the /16 mask, A is 'fooled': 172.16.100.1 AND /16 = 172.16.0.0 = 172.16.10.1 AND /16; A concludes B is local and ARPs for B, as it would for any host on network 172.16.0.0.

slides.title: Proxy ARP, example (2 of 3): R1 steps in
notes: R1's interface on A's link receives the ARP Request broadcast. Normally the router would discard it, since the target IP is not its own. With Proxy ARP enabled on the interface, the proxy process consults R1's route table: there is a route to 172.16.100.1 (subnet 172.16.100.0/24 is connected to the other interface) and it does not leave through the same interface the request arrived on. Therefore R1 can serve as the next hop for A.

slides.title: Proxy ARP, example (3 of 3): R1 answers with its own MAC
notes: R1 sends an ARP Reply to A placing the MAC of its own interface in place of B's MAC. A, believing the network is flat, receives the reply as if it came from B and records '172.16.100.1 → MAC R1' in its cache. From then on, A's frames to B go to R1, which routes them normally. Over time, A's cache accumulates several remote IPs mapped to R1's same MAC: the classic signature of Proxy ARP in action, useful in troubleshooting.

slides.title: ARP in 2026: gratuitous ARP, cache, security and IPv6
notes: Four topics that did not exist or did not matter in 1999. (1) Gratuitous ARP: a host announces its own IP/MAC pair (request or reply with sender = target); used to detect duplicate IPs, to update caches after a NIC swap and, crucially, by VRRP/HSRP and by VM migrations, to redirect traffic to the new owner of the IP. (2) Timers: Linux considers an entry 'reachable' for about 30 s (base_reachable_time, randomized between 15 and 45 s) and then revalidates it; Cisco IOS keeps entries for 4 h; VMs and containers create many entries. (3) Security: ARP does not authenticate; cache poisoning allows traffic interception; the standard defense is Dynamic ARP Inspection with DHCP snooping on the switches. (4) IPv6 does not use ARP: Neighbor Discovery (ND, RFC 4861) uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Solicitation/Advertisement sent to a 'solicited-node' multicast, so only the stations with that suffix process the request; neighbor state is tracked (reachable, stale, probe).

slides.title: IP in a routed internetwork: a complete example
notes: Synthesis example from the original (slides 108 to 117). Follow the headers at every hop with the students: the IP packet (source and destination) does not change; the Ethernet frame (MACs) is rebuilt at every router; the TTL drops by 1 at every hop.

slides.title: IP in a routed internetwork: the topology
notes: Four LANs interconnected by routers W, X, Y and Z. User A (172.16.25.22) wants to communicate with user B (172.16.27.23) through some application (SSH, HTTPS). The hosts received, via DHCP, their address, the /24 mask and the default gateway: X for A (172.16.25.1), W for B (172.16.27.1). The MACs follow the RFC 7042 documentation range; in the original they were real Cabletron (OUI 00-00-1D) and Cisco (00-00-0C) addresses. Overview of what will happen: A determines that B is remote, looks up the default route and resolves X's MAC; X routes to W over LAN 26; W delivers to B on LAN 27. Six steps on the next slides.

slides.title: The data transfer process: the six steps
notes: Map of the six steps to be detailed: (1) A sends the initial packet to X; (2) X receives and processes the packet; (3) X forwards the packet to W (next hop); (4) W receives the packet; (5) W delivers the packet to B; (6) B receives the packet. At each step, note what changes (Ethernet header, TTL) and what does not (IP addresses, payload).

slides.title: Step 1: A sends the initial packet
notes: A builds an IP packet destined for B (172.16.27.23). To reach B, A has to go through X: route determination says 'remote', the route table gives the default route via 172.16.25.1, and ARP (already resolved) gives X's MAC. The Ethernet frame leaves A with destination MAC = X, source MAC = A; the IP packet, with the initial TTL (64 on Linux and macOS, 128 on Windows), goes inside the frame's data field. The Layer 2 link is between A and X; the Layer 3 packet is from A to B.

slides.title: Step 2: X receives and processes the packet
notes: X recognizes its own MAC in the frame and accepts it (frames for other MACs would be ignored by the interface). The Ethernet header is discarded; the IP packet is validated (checksum, TTL > 1) and, since the destination IP is not X's, it goes to the routing software. X consults its route table for the longest prefix matching 172.16.27.23: 172.16.27.0/24, learned by a dynamic protocol (or a static route), with next hop 172.16.26.2 (W) out the LAN 26 interface. Route determination here is based on the destination network, not the host.

slides.title: Step 3: X forwards the packet to the next hop (W)
notes: X knows the next hop for 172.16.27.0/24 is W (172.16.26.2), learned from periodic routing-protocol updates or a static route. X builds a new Ethernet frame on LAN 26: destination MAC = W (resolved by ARP on LAN 26, if not already cached), source MAC = X's interface on LAN 26. The original IP packet is encapsulated with no change to the addresses; only the TTL drops to 63 and the header checksum is recomputed.

slides.title: Step 4: W receives the packet
notes: W recognizes its MAC in the frame coming from X and discards all the Ethernet information. The network-layer information goes up to the routing software, which checks that the packet can be routed and looks up the route by destination prefix: 172.16.27.0/24 is directly connected to W's interface on LAN 27. Therefore, the 'next hop' is the final destination itself.

slides.title: Step 5: W delivers the packet to B
notes: W recognizes that the packet is destined for a directly connected network. To build the frame it needs B's MAC: it consults its ARP cache and, if there is no entry, sends an ARP Request on LAN 27 for 172.16.27.23. With B's MAC, W builds the frame: destination = B, source = W's interface on LAN 27, and encapsulates the original IP packet with TTL 62.

slides.title: Step 6: B receives the packet
notes: B recognizes its MAC in the frame and copies the packet into its buffers. B's network layer verifies that the destination IP is its own and, by the Protocol field (6), hands the segment to TCP, which by the port number (22) hands it to the SSH server. B's reply to A takes the reverse path, with B doing its own route determination (A is remote → gateway W) and its own ARP for W. Close by asking: how many ARPs happened in total? (A for X, X for W, W for B, and on the return B for W, W for X, X for A: up to six, all cached afterwards.)

slides.title: Host names: from the hosts file to DNS
notes: The original slide showed the Cisco command 'ip host name address', which maps names to IPs locally on the router (useful only to the router itself). In 2026 the topic is DNS: a hierarchical namespace (root, TLDs, domains), resolved by recursive query from the resolver configured on the host (via DHCP or RA); records A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), PTR (reverse), CNAME, MX, SRV, TXT; transport UDP/TCP 53, with DNS over TLS (853) and over HTTPS (443) for privacy and DNSSEC for authenticity. The hosts file (/etc/hosts, C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts) still exists and takes precedence over DNS on most systems, which makes it useful for testing and dangerous when forgotten.

slides.title: Proxy ARP configuration: vendor defaults
notes: In 1999 the slide compared Cabletron (disabled by default, configured in the 'Port Level Setup' of the IP General Config screen) and Cisco (enabled by default on every interface configured for IP; 'no ip proxy-arp' to turn it off). Today: Cisco IOS/IOS-XE still enables Proxy ARP by default on interfaces (check with 'show ip interface'); Linux disables it by default (sysctl net.ipv4.conf.<if>.proxy_arp); Junos disables it by default (proxy-arp restricted or unrestricted per interface). 2026 recommendation: leave it off unless there is a documented need; DHCP delivers the correct mask and gateway to the hosts.

slides.title: IP routing protocols
notes: The original covered RIP, IGRP and OSPF, with EGP and BGP on two slides. The 2026 version replaces IGRP with EIGRP, adds administrative distance, OSPFv3/IS-IS and expands BGP-4.

slides.title: RIP: Routing Information Protocol
notes: RIP is the most direct implementation of distance vector: every router sends its whole table to its neighbors every 30 s (v1 in broadcast, v2 in multicast 224.0.0.9), uses hop count as the metric and treats 16 hops as infinity, which limits the network diameter to 15. Timers (Cisco): update 30 s, invalid 180 s, hold-down 180 s, flush 240 s. Versions: RIPv1 (RFC 1058, 1988), classful, no mask; RIPv2 (RFC 2453, 1998), classless, with mask, next hop, authentication and multicast; RIPng (RFC 2080, 1997) for IPv6, UDP 521 and ff02::9. Status in 2026: RIP survives in very small networks, labs and simple devices; for everything else, OSPF or EIGRP. It is still the best protocol for teaching distance vector.

slides.title: RIP: origin and variants
notes: RIP was not born with TCP/IP: it was developed at Xerox PARC as the routing protocol of XNS (Xerox Network Systems) in the late 1970s. The 'routed' implementation in BSD UNIX 4.2 (1983) spread it across TCP/IP years before it was formalized in RFC 1058. Novell adapted the XNS RIP for IPX; AppleTalk's RTMP and Banyan VINES' RTP were variations. All those derivatives died with their protocols; the only RIP still alive is the IP one (v2 and RIPng). The value of the slide is historical: it shows how the same Bellman-Ford idea was reused in every protocol family.

slides.title: RIPv2: message format and what is new
notes: The RIPv2 message (UDP 520) has a 4-byte header (command 1 = request, 2 = response; version 2) and up to 25 entries of 20 bytes. Each entry carries: address family identifier (2 = IP), route tag (to mark redistributed routes), IP address, subnet mask (the big novelty, which enables VLSM and CIDR), next hop (lets a router point to a better router on the same link) and metric (1 to 16). Authentication occupies the first entry (AFI 0xFFFF): simple password in RFC 2453, MD5 in RFC 2082 and modern cryptographic algorithms in RFC 4822. Using multicast 224.0.0.9 instead of broadcast spares the hosts that do not run RIP.

slides.title: Administrative distance: choosing among route sources
notes: New slide. When the same prefix is learned from different sources (static, OSPF, EIGRP, BGP...), the metrics are not comparable (hops versus cost versus bandwidth). The router uses administrative distance (AD): a trustworthiness value per source; the lowest wins and only that route goes into the routing table. The metric only breaks ties among routes from the same source. The values in the table are Cisco's defaults and widely copied; Junos uses 'route preference' with a different scale (direct 0, static 5, OSPF 10, IS-IS 15/18, RIP 100, OSPF external 150, BGP 170). AD is also the tool for floating static routes (backup): a static route with AD 250 only enters the table if the dynamic route disappears.

slides.title: From IGRP to EIGRP
notes: IGRP (Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) was created by Cisco in the mid-1980s to overcome RIP's limitations, mainly the 15-hop maximum, using distance vector with a composite metric (delay, bandwidth, reliability and load) and multipath. It was classful and proprietary; Cisco removed it from IOS in 2005. Its successor, EIGRP (1992), kept the composite metric (multiplied by 256) and added the DUAL algorithm, which guarantees loop freedom and fast convergence without hold-down, triggered-only reliable updates (RTP), support for VLSM/CIDR, IPv6 and unequal-cost multipath. In 2016 Cisco published the specification as RFC 7868 (informational), allowing third-party implementations, but in practice EIGRP remains a Cisco-network protocol; OSPF is the multivendor choice. The original mentioned using IGRP to route ISO CLNP; that was Cisco specific and fell out of use.

slides.title: The EIGRP composite metric
notes: To compare two routes to the same destination, EIGRP computes a composite metric that can be understood as an expression of the total transmission delay. The full formula combines bandwidth (B), delay (D), reliability (R) and load (L) with weights K1 to K5 the administrator may adjust; by default K1 = K3 = 1 and K2 = K4 = K5 = 0, so only bandwidth and delay count, and reliability is not considered (as was already the case in IGRP). Bandwidth = 10^7 divided by the lowest bandwidth on the path in kbps; delay = the sum of the interface delays in tens of microseconds. The result is multiplied by 256 relative to IGRP (32-bit scale). Important: the bandwidth and delay values are the ones configured on the interfaces (bandwidth, delay), not measured; adjusting 'delay' is the recommended way to influence route selection.

slides.title: Example: the same topology with RIP and with EIGRP
notes: Consider the route R1 would use to send packets from network A to network B. With RIP, the metric is hops: the direct R1-R2 link (1 hop) wins, even though it is a 2 Mbps serial. With EIGRP, the composite metric prefers the path R1-R3-R4-R2, three hops at 1 Gbps (metric 3,328 versus 1,792,000). The original used 19.2 kbps versus T1 (1.544 Mbps); the speeds changed, the lesson did not: hops are a poor metric when links are heterogeneous.

slides.title: Loop detection: from IGRP's hold-down to EIGRP's DUAL
notes: IGRP used split horizon and triggered updates, without poison reverse; the early versions also used hold-down and the later ones 'route poisoning' (any path whose metric increased was treated as unusable until confirmed). EIGRP solved the problem definitively with DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm, by J.J. Garcia-Luna-Aceves): for each destination, the router keeps the feasible distance (FD, the best known metric) and, for each neighbor, the reported distance (RD, the metric the neighbor advertises). A neighbor is a feasible successor if its RD is lower than the FD: the feasibility condition mathematically guarantees that the path through it does not pass through me and therefore cannot loop. If the successor fails and a feasible successor exists, the switch is local and instantaneous; if none exists, the router goes 'active' and sends queries to its neighbors, which reply; the route converges when all replies arrive.

slides.title: Multipath routing (ECMP and unequal cost)
notes: IGRP kept a list of possible paths in memory, not just one per destination, which allowed switching to the backup path on failure and splitting load across equal-cost paths. Today every IGP does ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path): routes with identical metrics are installed together (4 to 64, depending on the platform) and packets are distributed by hashing the 5-tuple, so a TCP flow is never reordered (RFC 2991/2992). EIGRP goes further with 'variance': it also accepts paths up to N times worse than the best, as long as they are feasible successors, and splits load proportionally. Modern data centers depend on ECMP over BGP in leaf-spine fabrics.

slides.title: Route redistribution (1 of 3): two routing domains
notes: Scenario: the company runs RIP in the old part of the network (R1, R2) and EIGRP in the new part (R4, R5); R3 takes part in both processes. Without redistribution, each router knows only the networks of its own domain, plus the connected ones: R1 cannot reach D, E and F; R5 cannot reach A, B and C. Only R3 knows everything, having routes from both sources. Redistribution is the mechanism that injects routes learned by one process into the advertisements of the other. Sources in the tables: C = connected, R = RIP, D = EIGRP (the notation of Cisco's 'show ip route'). EIGRP metrics are illustrative values.

slides.title: Route redistribution (2 of 3): EIGRP → RIP
notes: R3 is configured to redistribute the routes learned by EIGRP into the RIP process. Since the metrics are incompatible (3,072 does not fit in 'hops'), a seed metric must be set for the redistributed routes, for example 1 hop; R2 will see them with 2 and R1 with 3. Without the seed metric, many implementations drop the routes (RIP) or mark them unreachable. Now R1 and R2 reach D, E and F through the route via R3.

slides.title: Route redistribution (3 of 3): both directions and the risks
notes: Mutual redistribution is completed: R3 also injects the RIP routes into EIGRP, with a seed metric expressed in EIGRP's five components (bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, MTU), and R4/R5 start reaching A, B and C. Mutual redistribution is powerful and dangerous: a route can return to its domain of origin with a better metric (route feedback) and create loops or suboptimal paths. Standard defenses: use route tags to avoid redistributing back what came from the other side, filter with prefix lists, and adjust administrative distance (external EIGRP has AD 170 precisely to lose against RIP, 120, in case of feedback). Whenever possible, prefer a single IGP or one-way redistribution with a default route in the other direction.

slides.title: OSPF: Open Shortest Path First
notes: As the acronym says, OSPF has two primary characteristics: it is 'open' (a public specification, from the IETF) and based on the Shortest Path First algorithm (Dijkstra). It was developed by the IETF OSPF working group in the late 1980s (OSPFv1, RFC 1131, 1989; OSPFv2, RFC 1247, 1991; current version RFC 2328, 1998) because RIP was increasingly unable to serve large, heterogeneous internetworks: 15-hop limit, slow convergence, hop metric, no VLSM (v1). In 2026 OSPFv2 is still the most used IGP in enterprise networks; OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) routes IPv6 (and also IPv4, through address families, RFC 5838).

slides.title: OSPF: protocol overview (1 of 2)
notes: Three principles: (1) every router maintains a database (LSDB) describing the topology of the autonomous system, or rather of the area; (2) every router runs exactly the same algorithm (SPF) in parallel over that database, each with itself as the root; (3) in the original specification, OSPF computed separate routes for each type of service (ToS); that was removed in RFC 2328 because it was never usefully implemented. Today service differentiation is done by QoS and traffic engineering (MPLS-TE, Segment Routing), not by the IGP. Synchronization of the LSDB between adjacent neighbors uses Database Description, Link State Request, Update and Acknowledgment packets; the exchange is reliable (every LSA is acknowledged).

slides.title: OSPF: protocol overview (2 of 2)
notes: Four more characteristics: (1) OSPF allows sets of networks to be grouped into areas, whose topology is hidden from the rest of the AS, reducing routing traffic and LSDB size; (2) it supports flexible configuration of IP subnets (VLSM and CIDR) from the start, since every route carries a mask; (3) all protocol exchanges can be authenticated: null, simple password or cryptographic (MD5 in RFC 2328; HMAC-SHA in RFC 5709); in OSPFv3 authentication uses IPsec (RFC 4552) or the Authentication Trailer (RFC 7166); (4) externally derived routes (from another AS or another protocol, via redistribution) are carried transparently throughout the AS, marked as external, with tags.

slides.title: OSPF topology: backbone and areas
notes: Area 0 (the backbone) is the center: every other area must connect directly to it through area border routers (ABRs), and traffic between two non-backbone areas always passes through area 0. When an area cannot physically connect to the backbone, a virtual link crosses a transit area; it is a temporary fix, not a design. Area types: normal, stub (no type 5 external routes; receives a default route), totally stubby (also no inter-area routes), NSSA (a stub that can still inject externals via type 7 LSAs). In 2026, with routers able to hold huge LSDBs, many enterprise networks use a single area 0; areas remain valuable in very large networks or with unstable links.

slides.title: OSPF router classification
notes: Four roles, not mutually exclusive: internal router (all interfaces in the same area); backbone router (at least one interface in area 0); area border router, ABR (interfaces in more than one area, one of them the backbone; keeps one LSDB per area and summarizes between them); AS boundary router, ASBR (injects external routes, by redistribution or BGP). An ABR is always also a backbone router; an ASBR can be in any area (except stub).

slides.title: Network types supported by OSPF
notes: OSPF adapts its behavior to the link type: point-to-point (two routers; direct adjacency, no DR; Hello 10 s); broadcast multi-access (Ethernet; discovers neighbors by multicast and elects DR/BDR; Hello 10 s); non-broadcast multi-access, NBMA (Frame Relay, ATM, X.25 in 1999; neighbors configured manually, DR elected, Hello 30 s); point-to-multipoint (treats the cloud as a set of p2p links). In 2026 WAN links are Ethernet or tunnels, and the recommended practice on router-to-router links over Ethernet is to configure 'ip ospf network point-to-point', eliminating the DR election and speeding up the adjacency.

slides.title: The Hello protocol
notes: OSPF routers use Hello packets to discover other routers with interfaces on the same network (neighbors) and to maintain the relationship. Hellos are sent periodically (10 s on broadcast and p2p; 30 s on NBMA) to multicast 224.0.0.5; if no Hello arrives during the dead interval (4× Hello), the neighbor is declared down. To form a neighborship, some Hello parameters must match: area ID, Hello and dead intervals, authentication type and key, network mask (on broadcast links), stub-area flags. The MTU is compared later, during the Database Description exchange. On multi-access networks the Hello also elects the designated router (DR) and the backup (BDR). With BFD (RFC 5880) failure detection drops to tens of milliseconds without lowering the OSPF timers.

slides.title: Neighbors and adjacencies
notes: Neighbors are routers that discovered each other through Hello; adjacent routers are neighbors that synchronized their LSDBs and exchange LSAs with each other. Not every pair of neighbors becomes adjacent: on point-to-point links and virtual links, the two always become adjacent; on multi-access networks, each router forms an adjacency only with the DR and the BDR, and the others (DROthers) stay in the 2-Way state with each other. Adjacencies control the distribution of protocol packets: an LSA is flooded only over adjacencies. States of the neighbor state machine: Down, Attempt (NBMA), Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full.

slides.title: Designated router (DR) and backup (BDR)
notes: Every multi-access network has a designated router, elected by Hello: highest interface priority (0 = never), tie broken by the highest router ID; the election is not preemptive (a new router with a higher priority does not displace the current DR). The DR generates the network LSA (type 2) that represents the multi-access network in the LSDB and is the hub of synchronization: every router sends its LSAs to the DR/BDR (224.0.0.6) and the DR refloods them to everyone (224.0.0.5). Without a DR, n routers would need n(n-1)/2 adjacencies; with DR and BDR, 2(n-2)+1. Fewer adjacencies mean less routing traffic and a smaller LSDB (the network LSA replaces n² link descriptions).

slides.title: Link-state advertisements (LSAs) and the LSDB
notes: LSAs are flooded throughout the area, ensuring every router in the area has exactly the same topological database (LSDB), made of the LSAs from each router in the area. From the LSDB, each router computes the shortest-path tree with itself as the root; from that tree comes the intra-area routing table. Every LSA has a sequence number (to detect the most recent), an age (LS Age; re-sent every 30 min, LSRefreshTime; discarded at 60 min, MaxAge) and a checksum. Main types: 1 (router: the router's links, area scope), 2 (network: generated by the DR), 3 (network summary: generated by the ABR for routes from other areas), 4 (ASBR summary: where the ASBR is), 5 (AS external: generated by the ASBR, scope of the whole AS except stubs), 7 (NSSA external, converted to 5 by the ABR). OSPFv3 renumbers and adds types 8 (link) and 9 (intra-area prefix).

slides.title: Inter-area routing
notes: Each ABR summarizes the topology of its attached areas in type 3 LSAs (prefixes and costs only, not the topology) and transmits them over the backbone to all other ABRs; thus every ABR computes paths to destinations outside its areas. The ABRs then advertise those paths (again as type 3) inside their areas, enabling routing to other areas. Inter-area computation is a distance vector over the backbone (hence the requirement that every area touch area 0). Manual summarization at the boundary (area range) reduces the number of type 3 LSAs; stub and totally stubby areas receive only a default route from the ABR instead of the external and inter-area routes.

slides.title: AS external routes
notes: Routers that have information about other ASs (or about static routes and other protocols, redistributed) are ASBRs and flood that information throughout the AS in type 5 LSAs. To use an external route, every router needs to know how to reach the ASBR that advertised it; that is why the ABRs generate type 4 LSAs describing the location of the ASBRs. Two kinds of external metric: E1 (external cost + internal cost to the ASBR; compares paths fully) and E2 (default; external cost only, the same across the AS; tie broken by the internal cost). Stub areas do not receive type 5 and use the ABR's default route; NSSAs use type 7, converted to 5 by the ABR.

slides.title: OSPFv3 and IS-IS: the link-state IGPs in 2026
notes: New slide. OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) adapts OSPF to IPv6: it runs per link (not per subnet) using link-local addresses as next hop, removes addressing from the router and network LSAs (which now describe topology only) and creates type 8 (link) and type 9 (intra-area prefix) LSAs for prefixes; with address families (RFC 5838) it can also route IPv4, allowing a single protocol in dual stack. IS-IS (ISO 10589; RFC 1195 for IP; RFC 5308 for IPv6) offers the same algorithm with direct Layer 2 encapsulation (no IP), two hierarchical levels (L1 intra-area, L2 backbone), NSAP identifiers and TLV extensibility, which made it the preferred IGP of large providers and the base of Segment Routing (SR-MPLS and SRv6).

slides.title: Interior and exterior routing protocols
notes: Inside an autonomous system (AS 100 in the diagram) run the interior protocols (IGPs): RIP, EIGRP, OSPF, IS-IS, which optimize paths by metric. Between autonomous systems, on the Internet, runs the exterior protocol (EGP, in the generic sense): today exclusively BGP-4, which decides by policy (who is a customer, who is a provider, who is a peer) and not just by metric. The original listed IGRP among the interior ones and EGP among the exterior ones; both are legacy.

slides.title: Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP): the predecessor
notes: EGP (RFC 904, 1984) was designed for a very specific topology: it assumed a 'core' system of the Internet (the ARPANET) to which the various ASs attached, each through a single router, forming a tree. It did not allow multiple paths from an AS to the core, did not detect loops (which is why the topology had to be a tree) and only reported reachability, with no comparable metric. When the Internet stopped having a single core (NSFNET, commercial providers, early 1990s), EGP became unworkable and was replaced by BGP; in 1999 the slide said 'BGP is slowly replacing EGP'; the replacement was complete by the mid-1990s. The acronym EGP survives only as a generic term for 'exterior protocol'.

slides.title: BGP-4: the routing protocol of the Internet
notes: BGP was developed to overcome EGP's limitations as the Internet grew (BGP-1 in 1989, RFC 1105; BGP-4 in 1994, RFC 1654; current version RFC 4271, 2006). Unlike EGP, it detects loops: every advertisement carries the list of ASs traversed (AS_PATH) and a router rejects any route whose path already contains its own AS. It is a path-vector, policy-oriented protocol that runs over TCP (port 179) with explicitly configured sessions between peers: eBGP between different ASs (normally direct neighbors) and iBGP inside the same AS (full mesh or route reflectors, RFC 4456). With multiprotocol extensions (MP-BGP, RFC 4760) it carries IPv6, MPLS VPNs, EVPN and much more; with 32-bit ASNs (RFC 6793) it solved the exhaustion of AS numbers. In 2026 the global table has about 1 million IPv4 prefixes and more than 200,000 IPv6 prefixes.

slides.title: BGP-4: attributes and best-path selection
