notes: Every BGP route carries attributes: well-known mandatory (ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP), well-known discretionary (LOCAL_PREF, ATOMIC_AGGREGATE), optional transitive (AGGREGATOR, COMMUNITY) and optional non-transitive (MED, ORIGINATOR_ID, CLUSTER_LIST). Policy is implemented by manipulating attributes: LOCAL_PREF to prefer an exit inside the AS, AS_PATH prepending to discourage an entry, MED to suggest an entry point to the neighbor, communities to tag routes (RFC 1997, large communities RFC 8092). The selection order shown is Cisco's (RFC 4271 defines it from LOCAL_PREF on); other vendors differ in details (Junos has no 'weight'). Security: prefix and AS_PATH filters, prefix limits, RPKI/ROV (RFC 6811) to validate the origin; BGPsec exists but is little deployed.

slides.title: Controlling IP access
notes: The ACL examples use the classic Cisco IOS syntax, being the most widespread and the same as the original; the concepts (wildcard mask, implicit deny, direction, placement) apply to any vendor.

slides.title: ACLs in the router's processing flow
notes: An access control list is an ordered sequence of 'permit' or 'deny' rules evaluated top to bottom; the first match decides, and at the end there is an implicit deny of everything. Applied to an interface in a direction (in or out), the ACL is consulted before routing (inbound) or after it (outbound), silently discarding (or with ICMP 'administratively prohibited') the denied packets. ACLs also serve purposes other than filtering: selecting traffic for NAT, QoS, VPN, route-maps and management access (vty).

slides.title: Standard ACL example (1 of 3): permit only the internal network
notes: Standard ACLs (numbered 1 to 99, or named) filter by source IP address only. The wildcard mask is the inverse of the subnet mask: 0 = the bit must match, 1 = don't care; 0.0.255.255 matches any address starting with 172.16. List 1 permits traffic sourced in 172.16.0.0/16 and, through the implicit deny, drops everything else. Applied outbound on E0 and E1, it prevents traffic coming from the external network (through S0) from reaching the LANs, while traffic between the two internal LANs still passes. 2026 note: 'ip access-group ... out' still exists; to protect LANs from external traffic, the natural place is inbound on S0 (a single ACL) or a stateful firewall.

slides.title: Standard ACL example (2 of 3): deny a specific host
notes: Now ACL 1 denies host 172.16.10.254 (wildcard 0.0.0.0: every bit must match; 'host 172.16.10.254' is the shorthand) and permits everything else (0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255, or 'any'). Applied outbound on E0, it stops that host from reaching network 172.16.20.0/24, but not from talking to the external network or to its own LAN. Order matters: if the permit any came first, the deny would never be evaluated.

slides.title: Standard ACL example (3 of 3): deny a subnet
notes: Variant: deny the whole subnet 172.16.10.0/24 (wildcard 0.0.0.255) and permit the rest, applied outbound on E0. No host on LAN 10 reaches LAN 20; LAN 20 and the external network still reach LAN 10 (the ACL looks only at the source and only outbound on E0). It is a classic example of the limitation of standard ACLs: to allow only HTTPS from LAN 10 to a server on LAN 20 you would need an extended ACL.

slides.title: ACLs in 2026: extended, named, IPv6 and stateful firewalls
notes: Extended ACLs (100 to 199 or named) filter by protocol, source, destination and ports, and should be placed close to the source (to drop early); standard ACLs, source only, go close to the destination (to avoid blocking too much). Named ACLs allow editing rules by sequence number. In IPv6, 'ipv6 access-list' has a similar syntax with prefixes; be careful not to block ICMPv6 (ND, PMTUD), without which IPv6 does not work (RFC 4890). The fundamental limitation of ACLs: they are stateless; to allow replies to connections initiated from inside without opening everything, stateful inspection is used (zone-based firewall, NGFW), which tracks the 5-tuple and the TCP state. In 'zero trust' architectures, filtering moves to microsegmentation by workload identity, but the principle of ordered rules with an implicit deny remains.

slides.title: Additional IP routing topics
notes: Four operational topics from the original (slides 157 to 163), with updated Cisco commands and equivalents on other platforms.

slides.title: IP broadcast handling: the DHCP problem
notes: Question from the original: what does the router do with a BootP request (today, a DHCP Discover) sent in broadcast by a station with no address, if the server is on another subnet? By default, nothing: routers do not forward broadcasts (255.255.255.255), and that is one of the reasons they exist. Without intervention, the client would never get an address. Solutions: a DHCP server per subnet (impractical) or configuring the router to forward certain broadcasts as unicast to the server: the relay agent (RFC 1542 for BOOTP; RFC 2131 for DHCP), called 'ip helper-address' on Cisco. The relay rewrites the destination to the server's IP, puts its own address in the giaddr field (so the server knows which subnet to pick the address from) and may add option 82 (RFC 3046) with circuit information.

slides.title: DHCP relay and directed broadcast: configuration
notes: On Cisco, 'ip helper-address' on the interface facing the clients does the relay; by default it forwards UDP broadcasts on ports 37 (time), 49 (TACACS), 53 (DNS), 67/68 (DHCP/BOOTP), 69 (TFTP), 137 and 138 (NetBIOS); 'ip forward-protocol udp' adjusts the list. The global 'ip forward-protocol' command from the original still exists. Equivalents: Linux with isc-dhcp-relay or dhcrelay; Junos with forwarding-options dhcp-relay; L3 switches with 'ip dhcp relay'. As for directed broadcast (e.g., 172.16.20.255 coming from outside), RFC 2644 (BCP 34, 1999) ruled that routers must NOT forward it by default, in response to 'smurf' attacks; IOS has disabled 'ip directed-broadcast' since release 12.0 and practically no legitimate use (remote Wake-on-LAN) justifies turning it back on without an ACL.

slides.title: Secondary addresses
notes: A secondary address assigns the same interface a second (or third...) IP address, on another subnet. Use cases from the original, still valid: (1) the subnet ran out of host numbers and immediate renumbering is not possible; (2) migration from a flat (bridged) network to a routed one, with several subnets coexisting on the same link during the transition. Limitations: hosts on the two subnets only talk through the router (even though they share the wire); routing protocols treat secondaries specially (OSPF advertises them but does not form adjacencies over them; EIGRP/RIP do not always send updates from secondaries); DHCP relay uses the primary as giaddr. In 2026 the right alternative is almost always a new VLAN with its own subnet; secondaries are left for short migrations. In IPv6 multiple addresses per interface are the norm, not the exception.

slides.title: Unnumbered interfaces (IP unnumbered)
notes: 'ip unnumbered' enables IP processing on a point-to-point interface without assigning it a subnet of its own: the interface 'borrows' the address of another interface on the same router (today almost always a /32 loopback), which must have an IP address. In 1999 the goal was saving subnets on serial links (every /30 spent 4 addresses). The concept came back strongly in 2026 in data center fabrics: 'BGP unnumbered' establishes eBGP sessions over the IPv6 link-local addresses of the links (RFC 5549, now RFC 8950), without configuring any IPv4 link address, with automatic neighbor discovery through RA; OSPF and IS-IS also operate on unnumbered links. Classic limitations: you cannot ping the interface directly nor use static routes with a next hop on it (the interface is used as the exit).

slides.title: IPv6: from 'IPng' to the dominant protocol
notes: In 1999 this topic was called 'IPng or IPv6' and was based on drafts (RFC 1883, from 1995). The 2026 edition follows RFC 8200 (2017, Internet Standard) and reflects an Internet where more than half of the accesses to Google already use IPv6.

slides.title: Why IPv6: from 'IPng' (1995) to RFC 8200 (2017)
notes: Why IPng? The notes of the 1999 original asked exactly that. The answer was already the exhaustion of the 32-bit IPv4 space (4.3 billion addresses, many of them wasted by the classes) and the growth of the routing table. In 1995 the IETF chose the SIPP proposal as 'IP next generation' (RFC 1752), published IPv6 in RFC 1883 (December 1995), revised it in RFC 2460 (1998) and elevated it to Internet Standard in RFC 8200 (July 2017, STD 86). The predicted exhaustion happened: IANA handed out its last /8 blocks on February 3, 2011; LACNIC exhausted its final phase in August 2020. Adoption, slow for 15 years, accelerated with mobile networks and the large platforms: on March 28, 2026 native IPv6 access to Google exceeded 50% for the first time (50.10%, Internet Society Pulse); in Brazil, APNIC Labs measured about 59% of users as IPv6-capable on October 5, 2026.

slides.title: Main differences between IPv6 and IPv4
notes: The original listed six groups of changes, which remain the canonical summary (RFC 8200, section 1): (1) expanded addressing and routing capabilities: 128 bits, allocation hierarchy, scalable multicast with scopes; (2) a new address type, anycast, which delivers to the 'nearest' member of a group; (3) header format simplification: fields removed or made optional, fixed 40-byte header; (4) improved support for options, through chained extension headers; (5) flow labeling capability (flow label) for differentiated handling; (6) built-in authentication and privacy (IPsec). Add for 2026: no fragmentation in routers (the source uses PMTUD), no header checksum, ND instead of ARP and broadcast, autoconfiguration (SLAAC) and several addresses per interface as the rule.

slides.title: The IPv6 header
notes: Eight fields, fixed 40 bytes: Version (4 bits, = 6); Traffic Class (8 bits: DSCP + ECN, as in IPv4); Flow Label (20 bits); Payload Length (16 bits, bytes after the fixed header, including extensions; jumbograms through an option); Next Header (8 bits, same values as the IPv4 Protocol field, plus those of the extensions); Hop Limit (8 bits, the renamed TTL, without the 'time' meaning); 128-bit source and destination addresses. Note what disappeared compared with IPv4: IHL (the header is fixed), Identification/Flags/Offset (moved to the fragmentation extension), Checksum (the link and transport layers already verify) and Options (extensions). Update: the 1999 slide showed a 4-bit 'Prio' and a 24-bit 'Flow Label', the RFC 1883 format; RFC 2460 changed it to an 8-bit Traffic Class and a 20-bit Flow Label, kept in RFC 8200.

slides.title: Extension headers
notes: The IPv4 options became extension headers chained through the Next Header field and processed only by whoever needs them: Hop-by-Hop (0; the only one examined by every router; jumbograms, Router Alert), Destination Options (60; examined by the destination, or by intermediate destinations if it comes before Routing), Routing (43; type 0 was deprecated for security reasons, RFC 5095; type 2 in Mobile IPv6; type 4 is the Segment Routing Header of SRv6, RFC 8754), Fragment (44; only the source fragments), AH (51) and ESP (50) from IPsec. The recommended order is the one shown. RFC 8200 also established that routers must not insert or remove extension headers in transit. In practice, packets with many extension headers are frequently dropped by firewalls and by forwarding hardware (RFC 7872), which limits the use of extension headers to the essential.

slides.title: IPv6 addressing: 128 bits, three types, no broadcast
notes: 128-bit addresses written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons; leading zeros in each group may be omitted and a single run of all-zero groups may be replaced by '::' (RFC 4291; canonical form in lowercase with the longest run of zeros compressed, RFC 5952). The prefix uses CIDR notation (/64). Three types: unicast (one interface), anycast (the nearest member of a set; syntactically identical to unicast) and multicast (all members of the group); there is no broadcast. The total of 2^128 addresses is the number the original displayed in its title: 340,282,366,920,938,463,463,374,607,431,768,211,456.

slides.title: IPv6 address types and scopes
notes: Reference table. Global unicast (GUA, 2000::/3) is routable on the Internet; unique local (ULA, fc00::/7, in practice fd00::/8 with 40 random bits, RFC 4193) is the equivalent of private addresses, without NAT; link-local (fe80::/10) exists automatically on every interface and is used by ND and by the routing protocols as the next hop; ::1 is the loopback and :: the unspecified address. Special addresses: IPv4-mapped (::ffff:a.b.c.d) for dual-stack sockets; 64:ff9b::/96 for NAT64; 2001:db8::/32 for documentation. Multicast ff00::/8 carries the scope in the second nibble (1 interface, 2 link, 5 site, 8 organization, e global); well-known groups: ff02::1 all nodes, ff02::2 all routers, ff02::5/6 OSPF, ff02::9 RIPng, ff02::a EIGRP, ff02::d PIM, ff02::12 VRRP, ff02::1:2 DHCPv6 agents and ff02::1:ffxx:xxxx solicited-node.

slides.title: Neighbor Discovery (ND) and autoconfiguration (SLAAC)
notes: Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) gathers into five ICMPv6 messages what IPv4 did with ARP, ICMP Router Discovery and Redirect: Router Solicitation (133) and Router Advertisement (134) to discover routers, prefixes, MTU and parameters; Neighbor Solicitation (135) and Neighbor Advertisement (136) to resolve addresses and verify reachability (NUD) and duplication (DAD); Redirect (137). Stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC, RFC 4862) lets a host, without any server, generate its link-local address, check for duplicates, receive the /64 prefix in the RA and form a global address with an interface identifier derived from the MAC (EUI-64, now discouraged for privacy reasons) or a stable random one (RFC 7217), plus temporary addresses (RFC 8981). The RA flags define the role of DHCPv6 (RFC 8415): M (stateful: addresses from DHCPv6), O (stateless: only DNS and options) and A (autoconfigurable prefix). The RA can also carry DNS servers (RDNSS, RFC 8106).

slides.title: IPv6 routing
notes: As the original anticipated, every IPv4 routing algorithm was extended to IPv6 with small changes: RIPng (RFC 2080), OSPFv3 (RFC 5340), IS-IS with multitopology (RFC 5308/5120), EIGRP for IPv6 (RFC 7868) and MP-BGP (RFC 4760, AFI 2); identical static routes; longest prefix match on prefixes of up to 128 bits. Of the 'new features' listed in 1999: policy-based provider selection exists through multihoming with BGP and provider-independent (PI) or provider-aggregatable (PA) prefixes; host mobility (Mobile IPv6, RFC 6275) was standardized but is hardly used, because mobility ended up being solved in the upper layers (QUIC, applications) and in the mobile networks; automatic re-addressing (renumbering) does work: prefixes advertised in RAs with 'preferred' and 'valid' lifetimes allow switching providers without reconfiguring hosts (RFC 4192). In 2026 practice, dual stack with OSPFv3/IS-IS internally and MP-BGP externally is the typical setup; IPv6-only networks with NAT64 are growing in mobile carriers and data centers.

slides.title: IPv6 flows and traffic class
notes: There may be several active flows from a source to a destination, plus traffic not associated with any flow. A flow is identified by the combination of the source address with a nonzero flow label; packets outside any flow carry a zero label. The current specification (RFC 6437) states that the source assigns pseudorandom labels per flow (typically per transport connection) and that routers must not change them; the main practical use is as input to the ECMP and link-aggregation hash without having to read the transport headers, which is valuable when there are extension headers or encryption (RFC 6438). The original idea of reserving resources per flow (with RSVP) never took off; service differentiation is done through the Traffic Class, which carries DSCP and ECN exactly as IPv4 does.

slides.title: Security in IPv6
notes: The two built-in options from the original are still there: the Authentication Header, AH (RFC 4302), provides authentication and integrity without confidentiality; ESP (RFC 4303) provides confidentiality and integrity (today ESP with an authenticated cipher, AES-GCM, is the standard and AH is rarely used). What changed was the status: the first IPv6 node requirements (RFC 4294) mandated IPsec; RFC 6434 (2011) downgraded it to SHOULD and RFC 8504 (2019) kept it that way. IPsec in IPv6 is as optional as in IPv4 and uses the same IKEv2 (RFC 7296). The real security of IPv6 lies elsewhere: the absence of NAT requires an explicit stateful firewall; neighbor discovery is as vulnerable as ARP (rogue RAs, forged NS/NA), mitigated by RA Guard (RFC 6105) and ND inspection in switches; privacy extensions (RFC 8981) prevent tracking by interface ID; and over-filtering ICMPv6 breaks PMTUD and ND (RFC 4890).

slides.title: IPv4 / IPv6 transition and coexistence
notes: New slide. Three families of techniques: (1) dual stack (RFC 4213): hosts and routers with both stacks; DNS decides (AAAA first) and the Happy Eyeballs algorithm (RFC 8305) picks the connection that answers first; it is the basis of almost the entire current Internet; (2) tunnels: IPv6 encapsulated in IPv4 (6in4, protocol 41; GRE; 6rd, RFC 5969) or IPv4 in IPv6 (DS-Lite, RFC 6333; MAP-T/MAP-E), used where one of the stacks does not arrive natively; (3) translation: NAT64 (RFC 6146) with DNS64 (RFC 6147) lets IPv6-only networks reach IPv4 servers, and 464XLAT (RFC 6877) takes care of IPv4-only applications on IPv6-only phones, the model adopted by large mobile carriers. Direction for 2026: IPv6-only networks with IPv4 as a service (IPv4aaS), including in data centers and campuses (RFC 8925 lets DHCP tell the host 'do not use IPv4'). Brazilian resource (in Portuguese): IPv6.br from NIC.br.

slides.title: IP multicast
notes: The original covered multicast on the basis of the MBone and DVMRP; the 2026 edition centers on PIM-SM, SSM, IGMPv3/MLDv2 and IGMP snooping, keeping DVMRP and MOSPF as history.

slides.title: Multicast: one sender, many receivers
notes: The notes of the original recalled that most high-level protocols (TCP, UDP, ISO TP) only offer unicast transmission: a node sends to one other node at a time. To deliver the same content to N receivers, unicast requires N copies at the source; broadcast delivers to everyone, including those who do not want it, and only within the link. Multicast (RFC 1112, 1989) delivers a single copy that the network replicates only at the branching points, and only to those who subscribed to the group (a class D address). Anycast, by contrast, delivers to a single receiver, the nearest one. Applications in 2026: carrier IPTV, distribution of financial market data, videoconferencing and signaling in corporate networks, service discovery (mDNS, SSDP) and, internally, the routing protocols themselves. On the public Internet multicast never became widespread; unicast CDNs took the place of the MBone.

slides.title: IPv4 (and IPv6) multicast addresses
notes: A class D address (1110 + 28 bits of group identifier) designates a multicast group: 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. IANA reserves ranges: 224.0.0.0/24 (link-local control, TTL 1, never forwarded: 224.0.0.1 all hosts, .2 all routers, .5 and .6 OSPF, .9 RIPv2, .10 EIGRP, .13 PIM, .18 VRRP, .22 IGMPv3, .251 mDNS); 224.0.1.0/24 (internetwork control: 224.0.1.1 NTP, .39 and .40 Auto-RP); 232.0.0.0/8 (SSM, RFC 4607); 233.0.0.0/8 (GLOP, derived from the ASN, RFC 3180); 239.0.0.0/8 (administratively scoped, RFC 2365, the '10.0.0.0/8 of multicast'). In IPv6, ff00::/8 with flags and scope in the second byte: ff02::1 all nodes, ff02::2 routers, ff02::5/6 OSPF, ff02::9 RIPng, ff02::a EIGRP, ff02::d PIM, ff02::12 VRRP, ff05::/16 site scope, ff3x::/32 SSM. Official registry: RFC 5771 and the IANA Multicast Address Space Registry.

slides.title: Mapping IP multicast addresses to MAC addresses
notes: So that an Ethernet NIC can filter the groups of interest in hardware, the IP multicast address is mapped to a multicast MAC deterministically (RFC 1112): the 23 least significant bits of the group address are copied into the 23 least significant bits of the MAC 01-00-5E-00-00-00 (the IANA block; bit 24 is always 0). Since the group has 28 bits and only 23 are used, 5 bits are lost: 32 different groups share the same MAC (224.1.1.1, 224.129.1.1, 225.1.1.1, ..., 239.129.1.1 → 01-00-5E-01-01-01), and it is up to IP to filter what the NIC let through. In IPv6 the mapping uses 33-33 followed by the 32 least significant bits of the group (RFC 2464). Switches with IGMP/MLD snooping use these MACs (or rather, the IP groups) to forward multicast only to the ports with members.

slides.title: IGMP and MLD: hosts say what they want to receive
notes: IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) is used by multicast routers to find out, on each link, whether there are members of a group. Versions: IGMPv1 (RFC 1112): join through a membership report, silent leave (the router finds out by timeout); IGMPv2 (RFC 2236): Leave message, group-specific queries, querier election (lowest IP); IGMPv3 (RFC 3376): reports with source lists (INCLUDE/EXCLUDE), the basis of SSM, sent to 224.0.0.22. In IPv6, MLD does the same over ICMPv6: MLDv1 (RFC 2710) corresponds to IGMPv2 and MLDv2 (RFC 3810) to IGMPv3. The querier router sends periodic Queries (125 s) to 224.0.0.1 / ff02::1; hosts answer with reports. Switches perform IGMP/MLD snooping (RFC 4541): they listen to reports and forward the group only to the ports with members, avoiding flooding the entire VLAN.

slides.title: Dense mode vs. sparse mode
notes: Two distribution models. Dense mode: assumes that most links have receivers; traffic is flooded across the whole network and branches without members are pruned (flood and prune), with the prune expiring periodically and the flooding starting over; simple, but it wastes bandwidth and state; protocols: DVMRP, MOSPF and PIM-DM. Sparse mode: assumes that receivers are few and scattered; nothing is sent until a router with members explicitly joins the tree (explicit join), built around a rendezvous point (RP) or a core; protocols: CBT (historical) and PIM-SM, dominant today, with its SSM and Bidir variants. In 2026 practically only PIM-SM/SSM gets deployed; PIM-DM survives in small networks and labs.

slides.title: Multicast routing algorithms and the RPF check
notes: Evolution of the algorithms (the original's list): flooding (resends out every interface, loops contained by remembering packets); spanning tree (a single tree for all groups, concentrates traffic); RPB, Reverse Path Broadcasting (used on the MBone: forwards a packet only if it arrived on the interface that leads back to the source along the shortest path, the RPF check, and resends it out the others); TRPB, Truncated RPB (does not send to leaf links without members, using IGMP); RPM, Reverse Path Multicasting (TRPB + prunes traveling up the tree: the basis of DVMRP and PIM-DM); Steiner trees (optimal in total cost, but NP-hard and unstable; never used in practice); CBT, Core Based Trees (one shared tree per group, rooted at a core; the conceptual predecessor of PIM-SM). The RPF check is the common element of all current protocols: a router accepts a multicast packet only if it arrives on the interface that the unicast table points to as the path toward the source (or toward the RP); this prevents loops without needing a TTL.

slides.title: Multicast routing protocols
notes: DVMRP (RFC 1075, 1988) was the protocol of the MBone: its own distance vector (similar to RIP, 32 hops) used only for RPF, with RPM and tunnels between islands; MOSPF (RFC 1584) extended OSPF with group membership LSAs, computing per-(source, group) trees inside the LSDB; both are historical. The MBone (Multicast Backbone, 1992) was a virtual network overlaid on the Internet to broadcast IETF meetings, space missions and concerts; it reached thousands of subnets and faded away in the late 1990s as native multicast and, later, unicast CDNs took over. The PIM family (Protocol Independent Multicast, developed by the IETF IDMR working group, as the 1999 notes pointed out) uses any unicast table for RPF: PIM-DM (RFC 3973, flood and prune), PIM-SM (RFC 7761, shared tree with an RP and optional SPT), SSM (RFC 4607, only (S,G) trees with 232/8 and IGMPv3, no RP) and Bidir-PIM (RFC 5015, bidirectional trees for many-to-many).

slides.title: PIM-SM in operation: RP, shared tree and SPT
notes: Typical flow: (1) a receiver sends an IGMP Report for group G; its last-hop router sends a PIM Join (*,G) toward the RP (rendezvous point), hop by hop, creating the shared tree; (2) source S starts transmitting; its first-hop router encapsulates the packets in unicast PIM Register messages to the RP; (3) the RP decapsulates, forwards down the shared tree and sends a Join (S,G) toward the source to receive the traffic natively, then a Register-Stop; (4) the last-hop router, on seeing traffic from S, may send a Join (S,G) directly toward the source (switchover to the shortest-path tree, SPT) and prune the shared tree. RP discovery: static, Auto-RP (Cisco), Bootstrap Router (RFC 5059) or Anycast-RP (RFC 4610) for redundancy. PIM uses IP protocol 103, Hello to 224.0.0.13 / ff02::d.

slides.title: RSVP: resource reservation (and what is left of it)
notes: RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol, RFC 2205, 1997) was designed so that applications could reserve bandwidth and delay along the path, in the integrated services model (IntServ). Its central characteristic, highlighted in the 1999 notes: reservations are receiver-oriented: the sender sends PATH messages describing the flow; each receiver answers with RESV, which travels up the multicast tree and merges with the reservations of other receivers at the first branch already reserved, so that a receiver's reservation does not need to reach the source. State is 'soft' (refreshed periodically). It scaled well in multicast, but requiring per-flow state in every router of the Internet did not scale; service differentiation ended up being done by DiffServ (DSCP). What survived was RSVP-TE (RFC 3209): the same protocol, with extensions, signals MPLS traffic-engineering tunnels with guaranteed bandwidth and explicit paths, including fast protection (FRR, RFC 4090). In 2026 even that is losing ground to Segment Routing, which needs no signaling.

slides.title: MPLS and VRRP
notes: The last two topics of the original were presented in three slides (MPLS in two, VRRP in one, with a single sentence). Here they get the treatment their current importance justifies: MPLS is the foundation of carrier networks and VRRP is ubiquitous in corporate LANs.

slides.title: MPLS: label switching
notes: The 1999 notes explained the motivation: the Internet offered a best-effort service with software routing, little traffic engineering and limited aggregation; MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching, RFC 3031, 2001) attacked that by forwarding on short, fixed-length labels instead of IP prefixes. A label is a 32-bit 'shim' header inserted between the link layer and IP (EtherType 0x8847): a 20-bit label, a 3-bit traffic class (formerly EXP, RFC 5462), the S bit (bottom of stack) and an 8-bit TTL. The ingress edge router (ingress LER) classifies the packet into a FEC and pushes a label; the core routers (LSRs) only swap labels by looking up the LFIB, without looking at IP; the egress LER removes (pops) the label, often already at the penultimate hop (PHP). In 2026 the original speed gain is irrelevant (ASICs route IP at line rate); MPLS remains for what labels make possible: VPNs, traffic engineering and transport of any protocol ('multiprotocol').

slides.title: MPLS terminology
notes: The five terms of the original, plus the ones that were missing. FEC (Forwarding Equivalence Class): a set of packets treated the same way, for example all those destined to a prefix, or to a prefix with a class of service; FIB: the IP forwarding table with one row per FEC, used at the ingress to decide which label to push; LSP: a label switched path, established for each route through the network; LDP (RFC 5036): the protocol that distributes labels between neighboring routers (TCP/UDP 646), one label per prefix of the IGP table; LIB: the label information base, which stores every label received from every neighbor for each FEC; LFIB: the compact table used by the data plane (incoming label → outgoing label, interface); LER and LSR: edge and core routers; PHP: removal of the label at the penultimate hop, saving a lookup at the egress. Alternatives to LDP for distributing labels: RSVP-TE (traffic engineering), BGP (VPNs, labels per prefix) and Segment Routing (labels advertised by the IGP).

slides.title: Example: FIB, LIB and LFIB of router R4
notes: Reproduction of the original's example (slide 182) with modern names. Topology: LAN A (10.1.0.0/16) behind R1, LAN B (10.2.0.0/16) behind R2, LAN C (10.3.0.0/16) behind R3; R4 is the core LSR, with interfaces 1 (to R1), 2 (to R2), 3 (to R3) and 4 (to R5, an alternate path). Through LDP, each router advertises to its neighbors the label it wants to receive for each FEC: R3 tells R4 'for 10.3.0.0/16 use label 30'; R4 chooses its own incoming label for the same FEC (20) and advertises it to R1 and R2. R4's LIB stores every label received (including those from R5, which are not on the best path); the LFIB only contains those on the path chosen by the IGP: label 20 in → swap 30, interface 3. Packets from A to C arrive at R4 with [20] and leave with [30]; those from B to C arrive with [21] (the label R4 advertised to R2) and also leave with [30].

slides.title: MPLS applications in 2026
notes: Four families of applications: (1) Layer 3 VPNs (RFC 4364): the provider carries the private networks of many customers over a common core, with VRF tables on the PEs, MP-BGP distributing VPNv4/VPNv6 prefixes with a label and route targets, and a two-label stack (transport + VPN); (2) Layer 2 VPNs: pseudowires (RFC 4447), VPLS (RFC 4762) and, today, EVPN (RFC 7432) with a BGP control plane, also over VXLAN; (3) traffic engineering: RSVP-TE tunnels (RFC 3209) with explicit paths, reserved bandwidth and FRR protection (RFC 4090) within tens of milliseconds; (4) Segment Routing: eliminates LDP and RSVP; the path is encoded at the source as a stack of segments (labels) advertised by the IGP (SR-MPLS, RFC 8660) or as a list of IPv6 addresses (SRv6, RFC 8986), with controller-driven traffic engineering (SR Policy). The 3-bit traffic class carries QoS across the core. Carrier MPLS remains the 'premium' corporate WAN, even with the advance of SD-WAN over the Internet.

slides.title: VRRP: default gateway redundancy
notes: The original summed it up as: 'protocol used as a backup router protocol'. The problem: hosts configured with a single default gateway are cut off if that router fails, even when another router is on the LAN (old solutions: Proxy ARP, ICMP Router Discovery, running RIP on the hosts). VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol; RFC 2338 in 1998, RFC 3768 v2 in 2004, RFC 5798 v3 in 2010 with IPv6) creates a virtual router identified by a VRID (1 to 255), with a virtual IP address and a virtual MAC 00-00-5E-00-01-{VRID} (IPv4) or 00-00-5E-00-02-{VRID} (IPv6); the hosts use the virtual IP as their gateway. Among the physical routers, the one with the highest priority (1 to 254; 255 if it owns the IP; default 100) is elected master and sends advertisements to 224.0.0.18 / ff02::12 (IP protocol 112) every 1 s (v3: centiseconds); the others stand by and, if the advertisements stop for about 3 intervals, the highest-priority one takes over, sending a gratuitous ARP with the virtual MAC to update the switches. Preemption is enabled by default. Proprietary equivalents: HSRP (Cisco, informational RFC 2281, 1998) and GLBP (Cisco, with load balancing). Combined with interface tracking (object tracking), VRRP also reacts to the loss of the master's WAN link.

slides.title: VRRP in operation: a failover example
notes: LAN 172.16.20.0/24 with two routers: R1 (172.16.20.2, priority 120) and R2 (172.16.20.3, priority 100) share VRID 10 with virtual IP 172.16.20.1 and virtual MAC 00-00-5E-00-01-0A. The hosts have gateway 172.16.20.1 and, when they ARP for it, receive the virtual MAC, answered by the master (R1). R1 sends advertisements every second; R2 listens. When R1 fails (or its WAN link goes down and tracking lowers its priority), R2 stops receiving advertisements, takes over as master after the detection interval, starts answering for the virtual MAC and sends a gratuitous ARP so that the switches move the virtual MAC to its port; the hosts notice nothing (same IP, same MAC in the cache). When R1 comes back, it takes over again through preemption. Design tip: alternate the master between VRIDs on different VLANs to use both routers; in IPv6, the same mechanism covers the default router advertised in RAs.
